questiontext.text:
Prove that \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is irrational. Drag the blocks you need into the box, in order. Not every block belongs in the proof.

[[parsons input="ans1"]] {"steps": {# parsons_encode(proof_steps) #}, "headers": ["Your proof:"], "available_header": ["Drag from here:"]} [[/parsons]]
[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A proof by contradiction starts by assuming the opposite of the statement: here, that \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is rational. Here is the complete proof.

  1. Assume, for contradiction, that \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is rational.
  2. Then \(\sqrt[3]{2} = \dfrac{p}{q}\), where \(p\) and \(q\) are integers, \(q \neq 0\), and the fraction \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) is in its simplest form.
  3. Cubing both sides, \(2 = \dfrac{p^3}{q^3}\), so \(p^3 = 2q^3\).
  4. So \(p^3\) is even. The cube of an odd number is odd, so \(p\) is even: \(p = 2k\) for some integer \(k\).
  5. Then \(2q^3 = (2k)^3 = 8k^3\), so \(q^3 = 4k^3\) is even, and so \(q\) is even.
  6. So \(p\) and \(q\) are both even, and \(\dfrac{p}{q}\) is not in its simplest form. This contradicts the choice of \(p\) and \(q\).
  7. So the assumption is false, and \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is irrational.

This is the proof for \(\sqrt{2}\) with cubes in place of squares. The fact it needs is that if \(p^3\) is even then \(p\) is even. That is true because the cube of an odd number is odd: \((2j + 1)^3 = 2(4j^3 + 6j^2 + 3j) + 1\).

Two blocks do not belong. Assuming that \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is irrational assumes what is to be proved. Squaring both sides is copied from the proof for \(\sqrt{2}\), but \(\left(\sqrt[3]{2}\right)^2 = \sqrt[3]{4}\), not 2.

node.description: Diagnostic: squaring copied from the square root of 2

truefeedback.text: Squaring \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) gives \(\sqrt[3]{4}\), not 2. In the proof for \(\sqrt{2}\) we squared to remove the square root; here, cube both sides.
To prove that \(\sqrt[3]{2}\) is irrational by contradiction, assume the opposite: that it is rational.
